div.head: CHn cor 6
div.ab: Omnia placita et omnia debita quæ fratri meo debebantur condono, exceptis rectis firmis meis et exceptis illis quæ pacta erant pro aliorum hereditatibus uel pro eis rebus quæ iustius aliis contingebant.

Omnia placita et omnia debita quae fratri meo debebantur condono exceptis rectis firmis meis et exceptis illis quae pacta erant pro aliorum hereditatibus vel pro eis rebus quae iustius aliis contingebant.

I remit all pleas and all debts which were owing to my brother, with the exception of my legal rents and the payments which had been agreed upon with regard to the inheritances of others or with regard to property which more justly belonged to others.

note.seg: Nach Eadmer verbriefte Wilhelm II. 1093 ähnlichen Schulderlass: debita remittantur, offensiones antehac perpetratae oblivioni tradantur; s. o. Einl. 7. Vgl. Gl Amnestie 4—5a.—Die firmae sind die durch Kronbeamte dem Fiskus geschuldeten und von diesem gestundeten Pauschalsummen, um welche jene die Einkünfte aus Landgütern, Städten, Baronien der Krone, aus Hundreds und Grafschaften sowie aus vakanten Prälaturen gepachtet hatten; vgl. Gl Pacht 11; Finanz 4

According to Eadmer, William II in 1093 granted by charter a similar remission of debts: debita remittantur, offensiones antehac perpetratae oblivioni tradantur; see above Introduction 7. Cf. Gl Amnestie 4—5a.—The firmae are the lump sums owed to the Exchequer by royal officials, and deferred by it, for which those officials had farmed the revenues from estates, towns and baronies of the Crown, from hundreds and shires, and from vacant prelacies; cf. Gl Pacht 11; Finanz 4

Offenbar in Gegensatz zu sua und rectis 6, 1 war diese hereditas (liegender Nachlass), zum Nachteil des richtigen Erben, von der Krone einem Fremden, der als Bestechung mehr Erbantrittsgeld bot, zuerteilt worden. Das Unrecht wird zugegeben, aber nicht gutgemacht; vielmehr zieht Fiskus von ihm Gewinn, etwa wie vom Wucher. Nicht gemeint sein kann verwirktes Erbe oder das von Sippelosen: beides würde nicht ‘gerechter anderen zukommen’

Evidently, in contrast to sua and rectis 6, 1, this hereditas (inheritance in land) had been assigned by the Crown, to the detriment of the rightful heir, to a stranger who, by way of a bribe, offered a larger relief. The wrong is admitted but not made good; rather, the Exchequer draws profit from it, much as it does from usury. Forfeited inheritance, or that of men without kin, cannot be meant: neither would ‘more justly fall to others’
